newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks advance, key decisions awaited.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks advance, key decisions awaited.

text.p: Tobacco stocks rallied again Friday, reacting favorably to news that a key court verdict was again delayed and encouraged by expectations that a complete litigation settlement package is only weeks away.

Shares of Philip Morris Cos Inc were up 2-3/4 at a session high of 44-3/8 in midday trading, while shares of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, parent of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, were 1-5/8 higher at 34-3/8.
The American Stock Exchange Tobacco Index was up 7.22 points, or 2.53 percent, at 295.06.

Tobacco shares got a big lift shortly after the opening bell Friday from the announcement that the judge overseeing the regulatory case between the industry and federal government had postponed his decision for a second time.

U.S. District Judge William Osteen presided over the tobacco industry's February court challenge to the start of federal regulation over cigarettes by U.S. Food and Drug Administration. A decision is now expected no sooner than April 23.

That news came after Wednesday's news that the chief executives of Philip Morris and RJR Nabisco met with attorneys for tobacco lawsuit plaintiffs, congressional representatives and others to reach a comprehensive settlement.
Osteen's move opens discussion on whether the delays more likely point toward a decision in favor of the FDA or for the tobacco industry.

Martin Feldman, tobacco analyst at Smith Barney, said the extra time indicates the judge is aware of the developments in the industry outside his courtroom and the effect his decision will have on those developments.
"He reads the papers. He's knows what's going," the analyst said.

Tobacco stocks are woefully undervalued to begin with, according to analysts, so a strong move upward can happen any time. The stocks trade at a market discount instead of a market multiple, and have fundmentals that far outstrip the value investors are placing on them, analysts say.

In a research report, Sanford C. Bernstein analyst Gary Black provides even more optimism. Black wrote that an overall litigation settlement would be sealed in four to eight weeks, culminating in legislation passed by Congress and signed by President Clinton.
The industry would pay $8 billion to $10 billion a year to a government fund, and pay for the cost with a retail price hike of $0.50 per pack of cigarettes.

"Professional negotiators who only get involved in landmark decisions (e.g. professional sports strikes, other mass-tort settlements) have already been called in by plaintiffs to 'close the deal,'" Black wrote.
The purported involvement of top-level negotiators "strikes us as an indication that this deal could come much quicker than most investors realize," he said in the report.
